Sure. I can explain the most common models of GPS: the first generation (GPS 1.0), the second generation (GPS 2.0), and the more modern, first generation Advanced GPS (GPS 3.0). Here are some basic bullet points for each:

GPS works by finding a reference point in space (通常是某一特定地点), called a “satellite location fix”. GPS receivers use this reference point (also called the “reference frame”) to determine their own location, as well as the location of all other GPS receivers in the same orbit. The devices use this data to generate a set of highly accurate but relatively coarse location coordinates. You can think of this as setting up GPS receivers on your house’s exterior with a large point, called a “reference point”, and using the receiver’s compass and accelerometer to find out where it is inside the home, and where all the other receivers are on the exterior. A precise map of this indoor location can then be used to calculate locations of all the receivers on the exterior.

Once the indoor location has been calculated, GPS receivers send out signals from their antennas to the satellite network, and receive signals from the GPS satellites. GPS receivers are very accurate and will only be 1cm out while sending out signals to satellites, but their accuracy will vary depending on how far away you are from a GPS satellite, and what other obstacles you may have in your path to the satellite. The information received from the satellite, including the type of transmission and information like satellites in the “star map”, is sent back to your GPS receiver, which interprets it and uses it to calculate your location. GPS receivers are often called “AGPS receivers” (Analog High Precision Positioning System) because it uses analog technology (like RF) to get a better level of accuracy than GPS satellites, but still uses GPS as the most accurate reference. In some areas, a special algorithm is also used to make the position updates more accurate and robust, called “COMPASS”. GPS is able to get very accurate (0.5m) and precise (0.3m) position data in areas with poor cellphone reception, but GPS 3.0 can cover over 98% of the earth’s surface. COMPASS has improved the robustness of position data by using more accurate measurements that are derived from many sensors. This information is not transmitted to satellites, but is instead sent internally and stored to create a 3D model of the sensor locations. This information is then used to improve the accuracy of the position data, as well as to create a model of the sensor’s surrounding environment (terrain, buildings, etc.), which can improve accuracy and accuracy of location of a GPS receiver in areas where it is far away from the sensors. The model is also used to create a map of obstacles in the area, which is very helpful while navigating.

The location data from GPS receivers also provides information about the earth’s “geoid”, the idealized spherical shape of the earth’s surface that has the minimal variation in height in the places where we rely on GPS most for navigation and location, including the oceans, oceanside mountain ranges, airports, military bases, etc. So far, geoid measurements are only accurate to about 3m, but the technology to make more precise and accurate measurements is improving all the time.

So that’s how GPS works. It’s not magic, because it’s still based on science and math, and relies on equipment that we have built and tested for many years, and also relies on people who are trained in using GPS equipment and who can interpret the location data from GPS receivers and interpret it in the context of their day to day lives.
